chunks: Muhammad ibn al-Hasan ibn Ahmad ibn al-Walid (may God be pleased with him) narrated to us. He said: Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Saffar narrated to us. He said: Ayyub ibn Nuh narrated to us. He said: Muhammad ibn Abi Umayr narrated to us. He said: Muhammad ibn Humran narrated to me from al-Sadiq Ja'far ibn Muhammad (peace be upon them both). He said:
Whoever speaks about his believing brother based on what his own eyes have seen and his own ears have heard — he is among those concerning whom God, Mighty and Majestic, said:
'Surely, those who love to see indecency spread among the believers will suffer a painful punishment in this world and the Hereafter.'

key_terms.أخيه المؤمن: His believing brother — emphasizing the bond of faith that makes exposure of his faults especially heinous
key_terms.الفاحشة: Indecency, obscenity, lewdness — here refers to the exposure and circulation of shameful acts
key_terms.عذاب أليم: Painful punishment — the severe consequence threatened in both this world and the next

ai.seo_question: Is it a sin to spread news about a believer's faults even if you witnessed them yourself?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) warns that even reporting what one personally witnessed about a fellow believer's faults constitutes a grave sin, placing the speaker in the category condemned in Quran 24:19. This teaching challenges the common assumption that personal testimony justifies spreading news of others' sins. The broader context is the inviolability of a believer's honor: Islam demands concealment of sins, not their publicization, regardless of whether one witnessed them firsthand.
